{{Short description|American mathematician (1930–2005)}}
'''John Rolfe Isbell''' (October 27, 1930 – August 6, 2005)<ref>Birth date from [http://genforum.genealogy.com/isbell/messages/2234.html an excerpt] of "The Harloe-Kelso Genealogy" by C. B. Harloe (1943), accessed 2011-03-23; death date from death announcement in the [[Buffalo News]], August 28, 2005, [http://files.usgwarchives.net/ny/erie/obits/bn-dn/2005/aug/bn-dn28aug2005.txt reproduced by usgwarchives.net], accessed 2011-03-23. {{harvtxt|Magill|1996}} also states his birth date as 1930, but {{harvtxt|Henriksen|2006}} states it as 1931.</ref> was an American mathematician. For many years he was a professor of mathematics at the [[University at Buffalo|University at Buffalo (SUNY)]].

==Biography==
Isbell was born in [[Portland, Oregon]], the son of an army officer from Isbell, a town in [[Franklin County, Alabama]].<ref>Harloe (1943).</ref><ref name="magill">{{citation|first=K. D. Jr.|last=Magill|title=An interview with John Isbell|journal=Topology Communications|volume=1|issue=2|year=1996|url=http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/c/06.htm}}.</ref><ref name="henriksen">{{citation|first=Melvin|last=Henriksen|title=John Isbell 1931–2005|journal=Topology Communications|volume=11|issue=1|year=2006|url=http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/d/64.htm}}.</ref> He attended several undergraduate institutions, including the [[University of Chicago]], where professor [[Saunders Mac Lane]] was a source of inspiration.<ref name="magill"/><ref name="henriksen"/> He began his graduate studies in mathematics at Chicago, briefly studied at [[Oklahoma State University–Stillwater|Oklahoma A&M University]] and the [[University of Kansas]],<ref>The [[University of Kansas]] had professors Ainsley Diamond and [[Nachman Aronszajn]], who had previously been professors at Oklahoma A&M. The two moved to Kansas after Oklahoma A&M had instituted a requirement that instructors sign a strict [[loyalty oath]].  Ainsley Diamond, as a [[quaker]], had refused to sign the loyalty oath.</ref> and eventually completed a Ph.D. in [[game theory]] at [[Princeton University]] in 1954 under the supervision of [[Albert W. Tucker]].<ref name="magill"/><ref name="henriksen"/><ref>{{mathgenealogy|name=John Rolfe Isbell|id=18496}}.</ref> After graduation, Isbell was drafted into the [[United States Army|U.S. Army]], and stationed at the [[Aberdeen Proving Ground]].<ref name="magill"/> In the late 1950s he worked at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] in [[Princeton, New Jersey]], from which he then moved to the [[University of Washington]] and [[Case Western Reserve University]]. He joined the [[University at Buffalo]] in 1969, and remained there until his retirement in 2002.<ref name="topnews">[http://at.yorku.ca/i/a/a/l/11.htm Announcement of Isbell's death] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110714072234/http://at.yorku.ca/i/a/a/l/11.htm |date=2011-07-14 }} in ''Topology News'', October 2005.</ref>

==Research==

Isbell published over 140 papers under his own name, and several others under [[pseudonym]]s. Isbell published the first paper by [[John Rainwater]], a fictitious mathematician who had been invented by graduate students at the University of Washington in 1952. After Isbell's paper, other mathematicians have published papers using the name "Rainwater" and have acknowledged "Rainwater's assistance" in articles.<ref name="PhelpsRainwater">The seminar on [[functional analysis]] at the University of Washington has been called the "Rainwater seminar".<p>{{cite journal|title=Biography of John Rainwater|first=Robert R.|last=Phelps|author-link=Robert R. Phelps|journal=Topological Commentary|volume=7|number=2|year=2002|editor=Melvin Henriksen|url=http://at.yorku.ca/t/o/p/d/45.htm}}</p></ref>{{anchor|Stanley|Enos}} Isbell published other articles using two additional pseudonyms, '''M. G. Stanley''' and '''H. C. Enos''', publishing two under each.<ref name="henriksen"/><ref name="PhelpsRainwater"/>

Many of his works involved [[topology]] and [[category theory]]:
*He was "the leading contributor to the theory of [[uniform space]]s".<ref name="topnews"/>
*Isbell duality is a form of [[duality (mathematics)|duality]] arising when a mathematical object can be interpreted as a member of two different [[category (mathematics)|categories]]; a standard example is the [[Stone duality]] between [[sober space]]s and [[complete Heyting algebra]]s with sufficiently many points.<ref>{{citation|title=Isbell duality|first1=Michael|last1=Barr|first2=John F.|last2=Kennison|first3=R.|last3=Raphael|journal=Theory and Applications of Categories|volume=20|issue=15|pages=504–542|year=2008|doi=10.70930/tac/i8yf6iby |url=http://www.tac.mta.ca/tac/volumes/20/15/20-15.pdf}}.</ref>
*Isbell was the first to study the [[category of metric spaces]] defined by [[metric space]]s and the [[metric map]]s between them, and did early work on [[injective metric space]]s and the [[tight span]] construction.<ref>{{citation
 | author = Isbell, J. R.
 | title = Six theorems about injective metric spaces
 | journal = [[Commentarii Mathematici Helvetici]]
 | volume = 39
 | issue = 1
 | year = 1964
 | pages = 65–76
 | url = http://www.digizeitschriften.de/resolveppn/GDZPPN002058340 | doi = 10.1007/BF02566944| s2cid = 121857986
 }}.</ref>

In [[abstract algebra]], Isbell found a rigorous formulation for the [[Pierce–Birkhoff conjecture]] on piecewise-polynomial functions.<ref>{{citation|first=James J. |last=Madden |url=http://atlas-conferences.com/c/a/c/v/66.htm |contribution=The Pierce–Birkhoff Conjecture |title=International Conference and Workshop on Valuation Theory |year=1999  |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110608074427/http://atlas-conferences.com/c/a/c/v/66.htm |archive-date=2011-06-08 }}.</ref> He also made important contributions to the theory of [[median algebra]]s.<ref>{{citation | last=Isbell | first=John R. | title=Median algebra | journal=[[Transactions of the American Mathematical Society]] | volume=260 | issue=2 | date=August 1980 | pages=319–362 | doi=10.2307/1998007 | jstor=1998007| doi-access=free }}.</ref>

In [[geometric graph theory]], Isbell was the first to prove the bound χ&nbsp;≤&nbsp;7 on the [[Hadwiger–Nelson problem]], the question of how many colors are needed to [[graph coloring|color]] the points of the plane in such a way that no two points at unit distance from each other have the same color.<ref>{{citation
 | last = Soifer | first = Alexander | author-link = Alexander Soifer
 | isbn = 978-0-387-74640-1
 | location = New York
 | publisher = Springer
 | title = The Mathematical Coloring Book: Mathematics of Coloring and the Colorful Life of its Creators
 | title-link = The Mathematical Coloring Book
 | year = 2008|page=29}}.</ref>

Isbell also proved that a [[commutative ring]] whose multiplicative [[semigroup]] is finitely generated must be finite. The contrapositive to this statement provides a novel proof that there are infinitely many [[Prime number|prime numbers]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Isbell |first=J. R. |date=1959 |title=On the multiplicative semigroup of commutative ring |url=https://www.ams.org/proc/1959-010-06/S0002-9939-1959-0109163-5/ |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=10 |issue=6 |pages=908–909 |doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-1959-0109163-5 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref>
